headline: High risk: shared filesystem and overlapping write/network capabilities make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write filesystems, and Agent A explicitly shares state via filesystem and git while Agent B shares via integrations. That creates a plausible content-bridging path where one agent can ingest the other's outputs as trusted text. No stronger shared channel is documented, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF Agent A writes instructions into repo files that Agent B later reads as task context
IF Agent B ingests shared workspace content without provenance checks
mitigations: Add a provenance header to inter-agent files
Separate worktrees or directories per agent
Require manual review before either agent consumes the other's output
Disable automatic parsing of free-form file content
requires-engineering: add content-signing or provenance tracking

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches source code, git history, shell environment, and files in cwd; Agent B touches source code, issue trackers, team chat, and docs. Because both have filesystem access and broad network egress, sensitive repo or workspace data can flow into external services through either agent's normal operation. The shared workspace makes leakage plausible in default use.
conditions: IF either agent is given secrets in the shared repo or workspace
IF either agent forwards file contents to its backend or integrations
mitigations: Remove secrets from shared workspace files
Use separate repos or clones per agent
Restrict network egress for sensitive runs
Rotate any credentials present in cwd before pairing
requires-engineering: enforce data-loss prevention on outbound content

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. Agent A shares state via filesystem and git; Agent B shares via integrations and parallel sessions. Concurrent writes to the same repo or workspace can overwrite each other or corrupt git state, and the overlap is broad enough that default use is dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git branch or working tree
IF either agent performs writes while the other is mid-edit
mitigations: Assign separate branches per agent
Use file-level locks or a single-writer policy
Pause one agent before the other commits
Keep one agent read-only on shared paths
requires-engineering: add orchestrator locking around git and filesystem writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B can act autonomously in a cloud workspace and has write scopes to GitHub, Slack, Linear, Jira, and Notion, while Agent A can generate code and modify git state. If B treats A's output as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into commits or external actions. The pair therefore has a default path from generated output to downstream action-taking.
conditions: IF Agent B uses Agent A's output without independent verification
IF Agent B converts A-produced code or facts into commits or messages
mitigations: Require human review before external actions
Add a verification step before B commits or posts
Limit B's write scopes during paired runs
Mark A's outputs as untrusted in prompts
requires-engineering: add automated cross-checks against source files

E_compliance.rationale: Agent A handles git credentials and runs on the invoking user's host, while Agent B handles repo deploy keys and integration tokens in a vendor-managed cloud workspace. That creates a compliance mismatch around credential handling and retention boundaries, even though no specific residency regime is stated. The risk is narrower than a residency breach but still material.
conditions: IF regulated or production secrets are present in either workspace
IF logs or retained artifacts include credentials or token-bearing content
mitigations: Keep regulated secrets out of both workspaces
Use short-lived tokens only
Purge logs and transcripts after the run
Separate cloud and local credentials
requires-engineering: align retention and access-control policies
